content: Genital infections caused by Chlamydia trachomatis are the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infections globally. Screening sexually active young adults to identify and treat asymptomatic infections may help reduce the transmission of chlamydia and prevent complications in the reproductive tract, particularly pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in women. PID can lead to serious outcomes such as tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects and safety of chlamydia screening compared to standard care in reducing chlamydia transmission and complications of infection in both pregnant and non-pregnant women, as well as in men. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Sexually Transmitted Infections Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, CINAHL, DARE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science, up to February 14, 2016. Additional sources such as the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry (ICTRP), ClinicalTrials.gov, conference proceedings, and reference lists of retrieved studies were also reviewed. Trial authors were contacted for further information. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adult women (both pregnant and non-pregnant) and men. These trials compared chlamydia screening interventions with usual care and reported primary outcomes such as C. trachomatis prevalence, PID in women, epididymitis in men, or preterm delivery incidence. Non-randomized controlled clinical trials were included only if no RCTs were available for a primary outcome. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Disagreements were resolved through consensus or adjudication by a third reviewer. Results were presented in forest plots, and meta-analyses were conducted when appropriate using a fixed-effect model to estimate risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A pre-specified sensitivity analysis was performed for the primary outcome, PID incidence, based on the risk of selection and detection bias. Six trials involving 359,078 adult women and men were included in the analysis. One trial was determined to have a low risk of bias across all six assessed domains. Two trials investigated the impact of multiple rounds of chlamydia screening on C. trachomatis transmission. A cluster-controlled trial conducted in the general population in the Netherlands found no significant change in chlamydia test positivity after three annual screening invitations (intervention: 4.1% vs. control: 4.3%; RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.09; 1 trial, 317,304 participants; low-quality evidence). However, the uptake of the intervention was low, with a maximum participation rate of 16%. In contrast, a cluster-randomized trial among female sex workers in Peru demonstrated a reduction in chlamydia prevalence after four years (adjusted RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.98; 1 trial, 4,465 participants; low-quality evidence). Four RCTs evaluated the effect of chlamydia screening on PID incidence in women 12 months after a single screening offer. When analyzed using the intention-to-treat principle, the risk of PID was lower in women in the intervention groups compared to the control groups, with minimal evidence of heterogeneity between trials (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.94; I² = 27%; 4 trials, 21,686 participants; moderate-quality evidence). A sensitivity analysis revealed that the estimated effect of chlamydia screening in two RCTs with a low risk of detection bias (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.17) was consistent with no effect and was smaller than the effect observed in two RCTs with a high or unclear risk of detection bias (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.83). In men, the risk of epididymitis 12 months after a single screening offer was 20% lower in those invited for screening compared to those not invited. However, the confidence interval was wide and included the possibility of no effect (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.42; 1 trial, 14,980 participants; very low-quality evidence). No RCTs were identified that evaluated the effects of chlamydia screening during pregnancy, nor were there any trials that assessed potential harms associated with chlamydia screening. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the impact of chlamydia screening on C. trachomatis transmission is of low quality due to issues with directness and risk of bias. There is moderate-quality evidence suggesting that detecting and treating chlamydia infections can reduce the risk of PID in women at an individual level. However, there is a lack of RCT evidence on the effects of chlamydia screening during pregnancy. Future RCTs should aim to evaluate the effects of chlamydia screening during pregnancy, the impact of repeated rounds of screening on the incidence of chlamydia-associated PID, and the rates of reinfection in both general and high-risk populations.
